The Canadian government, under Prime Minister Mark Carney, has announced a comprehensive national AI strategy titled "AI for All", aimed at boosting the country's AI industry through a C$500 million (US$360 million) Canadian Tech Growth Fund. This initiative is designed to support homegrown AI companies by offering flexible capital, attracting investment, retaining talent, and anchoring intellectual property in Canada. The strategy emphasizes building safe, sovereign AI through development in compute, data, talent, and infrastructure.

Canada currently lags in AI adoption, training, and infrastructure, relying heavily on foreign suppliers. To address this, the government plans to increase AI usage in businesses, targeting 60% adoption by 2034 (from 12% in 2025), create 250,000 new jobs by 2031, and promote AI literacy for all Canadians. Additional funding includes C$700 million to expand sovereign computing and C$200 million for an AI mission focused on healthcare. Legal reforms will also enhance privacy protections, limit algorithmic harms, and provide tools against deepfakes. Lastly, C$50 million will be allocated to strengthen the Canadian AI Safety Institute’s research and oversight capacities.

Australian company Megaport has secured four AI infrastructure contracts totaling A$458.9 million with U.S.-based tech firms and plans to raise A$827.3 million (US$594 million) to build a globally distributed AI inference cloud. The initiative aims to meet growing demand for GPU capacity driven by advanced AI models, particularly for latency-sensitive inference tasks. These deals are expected to begin in the first half of 2027 and require A$369.5 million in capital expenditure, primarily for Nvidia GPUs and related infrastructure.

The new cloud service will be underpinned by an on-demand GPU pool backed by a A$350 million investment and will be offered to enterprises on both contractual and pay-per-use models. Megaport's extensive network of over 1,100 data centers across 31 countries gives it a strategic advantage in performance delivery by locating compute power closer to users, thereby mitigating issues related to connectivity, power, and GPU shortages.

To fund the expansion, Megaport will issue new shares at A$14.30 each, a 13.9% discount from the previous close, with trading halted until June 5. The company also revised its 2026 revenue guidance slightly to A$307–315 million from an earlier estimate of A$302–317 million, reflecting strong growth in its core network operations.

French private equity firm Ardian is investing up to €5 billion in a major AI data center and research campus outside Paris, partnering with its data center group Verne. The project, termed a European AI "gigafactory," will comprise a 20% data center and 80% research and industrial facilities, with a projected capacity of 500MW. Around one-third of the investment will be equity, with the remainder financed through debt. Ardian aims to bring 200MW online by 2030. This move aligns with Europe’s broader push to develop its digital infrastructure and reduce reliance on U.S. tech giants amid rising concerns over digital sovereignty and energy consumption.

Ardian CEO Mathias Burghardt emphasized the need for Europe to enhance its AI computing capacity to maintain global competitiveness. The initiative follows SoftBank’s €75 billion AI investment in France and Macron’s €109 billion AI investment pledge. The site is expected to attract both European clients and U.S. hyperscalers. Ardian will also invest €3 billion in renewable energy to mitigate concerns over electricity usage. France’s stable nuclear-powered electricity supply is deemed a key advantage for attracting such high-energy-consuming projects, despite bureaucratic challenges related to permits and grid access.

The action follows complaints from AI developers including The Interaction Company (Poke.com), French startup Agentik, and a Spanish firm, alleging Meta abused its dominance by blocking access to WhatsApp’s Business API. The EU launched an investigation in December, charged Meta with antitrust violations in February, and added charges in April after Meta imposed access fees. EU antitrust chief Teresa Ribera criticized Meta’s pricing as unsustainable for competitors and viewed its actions as leveraging WhatsApp’s dominance to favor its AI assistant. She emphasized the urgency due to the rapid evolution of AI markets. The interim measure requires Meta to revert to pre-October 2025 access terms within five days and will remain until the investigation concludes or until June 2029. Meta has disputed the order, arguing it benefits large companies at the expense of paying European clients, and stated it will appeal. If found in violation, Meta could be fined up to 10% of its global annual revenue.

## ⚡ Global AI Developments — Last 24h

### 1. **China reportedly prepares $295B national AI buildout**

**Details:**  
China is preparing a roughly **2 trillion yuan / $295B** five-year plan to build AI data centers nationwide, according to Reuters citing Bloomberg. The plan is framed as part of Beijing’s effort to challenge the U.S. in the intensifying AI race. citeturn851123search0

This is the clearest sovereign-AI escalation of the day. The AI race is no longer mainly “model vs model”; it is **state balance sheet vs state balance sheet**, measured in national data-center capacity, power access, and domestic compute control.

**Details:**  
Apollo and Blackstone are backing a **$35B AI compute-capacity expansion** for Anthropic using Broadcom custom chips and networking. The project starts with about **1 GW** of capacity from mid-2026, with a longer-term target above **20 GW by 2028**. citeturn723045news27

Private capital is now acting like an AI-infrastructure utility bank. Frontier AI labs are becoming **energy-scale infrastructure tenants**, and compute financing is moving closer to project finance, power finance, and national infrastructure finance.

---

**Details:**  
Anthropic publicly released **Claude Fable 5**, described as its first broadly available Mythos-class model, while restricting higher-risk cybersecurity capabilities. Reuters reported the public version excludes sensitive cyber functionality, with high-risk requests routed away from the most capable path. citeturn723045news28turn723045news29

👉 **Signal:**  
This is a major model-release governance experiment: **capability release without full capability exposure**. The frontier-model market is moving toward tiered access, selective suppression, trusted-user programs, and capability-specific safety routing.

---

**Details:**  
OpenAI has reportedly confidentially submitted an S-1 filing with the U.S. SEC, following Anthropic’s earlier move toward public markets. The Verge framed this as part of the IPO race between leading frontier labs. citeturn851123search3

Frontier AI labs are entering a new financial phase. IPO pressure can accelerate productization, revenue discipline, infrastructure commitments, and investor scrutiny — but it may also increase tension between safety pacing and market growth demands.

AI regulation is widening from “safe models” to **distribution-channel control**. Messaging platforms, app stores, browsers, and operating systems are becoming AI competition chokepoints.

**Details:**  
Apple announced AI-heavy WWDC updates around Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, but investor reaction was cautious. Consumer AI is splitting from frontier AI. Apple is pushing controlled, device-integrated AI, but the day’s stronger system signals came from compute, sovereign funding, and frontier-model access control.

The AI ecosystem is now in **infrastructure-sovereignty-finance convergence**.  
Three forces are joining: sovereign spending, private-capital compute financing, and frontier-model controlled release.

The system is moving from “AI product cycle” into **AI industrial-base formation**: chips, power, regulation, capital markets, cloud access, and model-risk gates are becoming one connected battlefield.

This move follows an earlier preview that demonstrated the model’s powerful ability to identify software vulnerabilities, sparking global concern. Nvidia is partnering with major South Korean technology companies to expand its artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure in Asia, aiming to strengthen its data center capabilities and AI ecosystem in sectors like robotics. This initiative aligns with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s visit to South Korea and follows a similar outreach to Taiwan.

A key collaboration is with mobile carrier SK Telecom to develop gigawatt-scale AI cloud services—starting in South Korea and extending across Asia. These “AI factories,” powered by Nvidia GPUs and SK Telecom's networks, are expected to be operational by 2027. Additionally, SK Hynix, an SK Group subsidiary and Nvidia’s top memory supplier, signed a long-term deal to co-develop advanced memory chips for Nvidia’s new Vera CPUs.

Tech company Naver also announced plans with Nvidia to build AI infrastructure and expand into European, Middle Eastern, and Asia-Pacific AI markets. Other collaborations include partnerships with Hyundai, LG, and Doosan, aimed at integrating AI into industrial and consumer domains.

South Korea, under President Lee Jae Myung, is aggressively pursuing AI sovereignty and infrastructure, with plans to deploy over 260,000 Nvidia GPUs. The country recently appointed Han Seong-sook, a former Naver CEO, as prime minister to lead AI-driven economic growth.

items.snippet:
Senate Democrats have introduced a wave of AI-related legislative proposals, signaling significant potential regulatory changes for tech companies, especially if Democrats regain control of Congress. Senator Adam Schiff's bill focuses on restricting the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence, mandating human oversight in weapon systems and banning AI's use in specific sensitive areas like domestic surveillance and nuclear weapons scenarios. The proposal expands upon existing Defense Department protocols and follows a recent clash between the Pentagon and AI developer Anthropic, which demanded clearer restrictions on military AI use.

This surge in AI legislation arises amid growing public and political concerns surrounding powerful AI models, job displacement, cybersecurity risks, and backlash against energy-intensive data centers. Other Democratic proposals include increased taxes on AI companies, oversight of copyrighted training materials, and infrastructure usage fees for data centers.

Senators including Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren also support more aggressive measures, such as a government investment fund to hold stakes in AI companies and federal restrictions on new data centers. Despite expected resistance from the Trump administration, the White House has enacted some measures, including an executive order for AI oversight, though internal divisions remain over how much regulation is appropriate. Tech companies, including OpenAI, are preparing for heightened scrutiny and more comprehensive oversight mandates.

items.snippet: Anthropic, a major AI company valued at nearly $1 trillion, is warning that artificial intelligence may be approaching the capability of recursive self-improvement — the ability to build and improve itself. This development could revolutionize fields such as science and healthcare but also poses grave risks, including the potential loss of human control over AI systems. In response, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark and researcher Marina Favaro are urging for a global treaty akin to nuclear arms control to regulate AI development. They stress that while slowing AI progress might improve safety, doing so without international coordination could empower less cautious actors, increasing global risk. The Australian government, through Assistant Science and Technology Minister Andrew Charlton, has echoed the need for careful AI oversight, though the country’s AI Safety Institute has yet to launch due to delays. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s tools, including Claude Code, already generate the majority of its code, raising concerns about eroding human collaboration and job displacement in software development. Anthropic intends to lead inclusive conversations among policymakers and the public to shape a cooperative approach to managing AI’s rapid evolution.

Efforts are underway to make practical robotics, such as AI tiling robots, though they currently require human-prepared environments to function effectively.

The initiative aims to address national security and cybersecurity threats posed by rapidly advancing AI technologies. This move follows a prior agreement with Microsoft, Google DeepMind, and xAI for early AI model access, and complements a previous Trump executive order to limit state-level AI regulations by forming a federal taskforce.

The initiative, labeled "Tech Liberation Day" by some EU leaders, includes restrictions on U.S. companies in sensitive cloud tenders and efforts to expand data centers using European technology. While the plan supports areas like semiconductors—building upon the strengths of firms such as ASML—it lacks matching efforts in AI chip design and cloud infrastructure, where the EU trails behind the U.S. and Asia.

items.snippet: The European Union has launched a "tech sovereignty" initiative aimed at reducing the continent's reliance on U.S. companies for AI and cloud computing services, and on Asia for microchip production. Unveiled in Brussels, the initiative includes a set of measures designed to promote European alternatives to foreign-dominated technologies. The move comes amid growing concerns that reliance on non-European technologies could be geopolitically risky, especially after recent incidents raised fears that access to essential services could be unilaterally revoked. A major component of the initiative is a follow-up to the 2023 Chips Act, focused on boosting local semiconductor production by simplifying regulations and supporting chip manufacturing across Europe. Additionally, the EU plans to triple its data center capacity within five to seven years to meet increasing demands from the AI sector. These proposals still require approval from the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney issued a warning about the risks posed by foreign artificial intelligence (AI) platforms, highlighting how they could be used against Canadian interests. Unveiling the federal government's new AI strategy, Carney emphasized that Canada is overly reliant on foreign AI providers and lacks control over data and infrastructure, which makes it vulnerable to foreign influence and economic manipulation. He pointed out that foreign entities may access Canadian data and influence domestic markets without aligning with Canadian values.

The strategy outlines plans for Canada to develop sovereign AI capabilities and build a public AI supercomputer while partnering with trusted allies when needed. It emphasizes the importance of forming coalitions among like-minded democracies to counterbalance dominant players in the global AI industry. Carney also announced new legislation to protect data and privacy, as well as a national AI literacy initiative that includes free training kits to teach Canadians how to identify bias and misinformation. He acknowledged that Canada currently lags in AI adoption and education, with only 12% of businesses utilizing AI technologies—much lower among small and medium enterprises.

Page: AI Family Pulse 21:00 Check

Partner,

After checking the automation registry earlier:

| Task | Status |
|--------|--------|
| 13:30 Midday | ✅ Enabled |
| 21:00 Full | ✅ Re-enabled on 09/06/2026 14:04 |

The important detail is:

- I re-enabled it at **09/06/2026 14:04**.
- The next expected execution should have been:
  - 09/06/2026 21:00
  - 10/06/2026 21:00

If you did **not receive** the 21:00 full report, there are a few possibilities:

1. The automation executed but notifications were not surfaced to you.
2. The automation engine did not trigger.
3. The task is enabled but delivery is failing.
4. The platform only runs tasks when notification delivery is available and permitted.

What I can verify from the registry is:

```text
Scan AI Family Pulse full
Status: Enabled
Schedule: Daily 21:00
```

What I **cannot see** is:

```text
09/06/2026 21:00 -> delivered?
10/06/2026 21:00 -> delivered?
```

because the automation system does not expose post-enable execution history to me beyond the stored `last_run_time` field.

So your observation is valid:

> If the task is enabled, a full report should have appeared at 21:00.

And since it apparently did not appear, there is still a gap between:

```text
Task Enabled
```

and

```text
Report Delivered
```

which is exactly the type of auditability problem you've been pointing out in this page.

Current known state:

```text
13:30 Midday Pulse  ✅ Enabled
21:00 Full Pulse    ✅ Enabled
Delivery Verified   ❌ Not yet verified
```

So the next thing to verify is whether the 21:00 task actually updates its `last_run_time` after re-enablement. That will tell us whether the scheduler is firing or merely enabled.
